2611.18850.abstract: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) found more bright $z\gtrsim10$ galaxies than expected before its launch. No consensus has emerged on whether difficulties in reproducing them stem from missing physics, simplifying assumptions that break down at the highest redshifts, or model mis-calibration. This is complicated because most galaxy models cannot be compared like-to-like, and models invoking different physical processes can make similar predictions for compressed summaries such as ultraviolet luminosity functions (UV LFs). Here we describe galaxy populations in a universal language: a chain of physically and empirically motivated conditional distributions linking halo mass, stellar mass, star formation rate and UV magnitude, defined consistently across models and data. We build a broad prior from fits to five hydrodynamic simulations, which predict very different high-redshift galaxy populations. We infer the parameters of this flexible galaxy model from $z>6$ JWST observations of UV LFs and angular correlation functions (ACFs). Including the mass-complete ACFs disfavors a large scatter around the stellar-to-halo mass relation (SHMR). With simulation-based priors, the star-forming main sequence (SFMS) is described by a star-formation timescale of about one halo dynamical time, and the scatter around the SFMS increases toward lower stellar masses. The SFMS scatter is the main source of stochasticity in UV magnitude at fixed halo mass, accounting for a median $\sim$61% of the variance at $M_{\rm UV}=-20$ (SHMR scatter: $\sim$36%). Bayesian model selection finds no evidence for redshift evolution of the SHMR or for an SFMS slope different from unity. At $z\sim20$, our fiducial model predicts UV LFs orders of magnitude below estimates from photometric candidates. A consensus on the discrepant UV LF estimates at $z\geq14$ is needed to determine whether model extensions are required.

2611.18904.abstract: In accordance with the AGN Unification model, the optical variability of Seyfert 2s is expected to be suppressed because the central engine is obscured by a dusty torus. The absorbed UV/optical radiation is reprocessed and re-emitted in longer wavelengths including the mid-infrared (MIR), making MIR variability a promising probe of obscured AGNs. We investigate the optical ASAS-SN and MIR NEOWISE variability of Seyfert 1 and Seyfert 2 AGNs from the \textit{Swift} 58-month BAT catalog, comparing both populations against non-variable galaxies. One of the first systematic studies of MIR AGN variability, we detected significant variability for Sy1s and the majority of Sy2s. 65% of Sy2s exhibit variability as significant as Sy1s in the MIR, especially in the W2 band, indicating torus dominated MIR variability. Additionally, 22% of Sy2s show higher variability compared to non-variable sources in the W2 band with p-value of $7.1\times 10^{-15}$. Demonstrating MIR variability as an important method to probe the variability of torus and select obscured AGN. Finally, we perform dust reverberation mapping on the Sy1 sample between the optical and W1 or W2 light curves, with measured time delays between 22-786 days (0.02-0.61 pc) for the hot dust in the inner regions of the torus. Our measured torus radius-luminosity slope, $R \propto L^{0.42\pm0.05}$, agrees with literature results. Combining the W1 and W2 band lags with archival NIR measurements, we measured the temperature profile of the torus with $T \propto R^{-\alpha}$, where $\alpha$ values range from 0.3-1.1.

2611.18929.title: Quantifying the Dominance and Emergence of Brightest Cluster Galaxies in SPT and Planck Clusters: A Novel Application of the Gini Index

figures.caption: Figure 1: An illustration of the calculation of the Gini index. The Lorenz curves for the idealized $\rm G=0$ and $\rm G=1$ cases are plotted, as well as those for two galaxy clusters with $\rm G=0.63$ (dashes) and $\rm G=0.95$ (dots). The Gini index is calculated by doubling the area between the 1:1 line of perfect equality and Lorenz curve and then applying the finite sample normalization factor, $\rm N/(N-1)$.

Figure 2: The evolution of the $\rm G$ini index with a varying limiting magnitude ($\rm M_{lim}$) and a varying flat cluster richness (N) cut, applied here to the Blanton et al. [15] SDSS r-band Schechter function. Given the application to the luminosity function, this figure displays the distribution of the minimum Gini index, $\rm G_{min}$ (equivalently $\rm G_{field}$) compared to the limiting magnitude and richness, but the trends apply generally. We show the median $\rm G_{min}$ with 68% and 95% confidence intervals, calculated by sampling $\rm\Phi(M)$ above $\rm M_{lim}$ and measure G for 10,000 bootstrapping iterations. When limiting richness, we fix $\rm M_{lim}=M^{*}+1.75$. While the Gini index is largely independent of Schechter model parameters, and thus band and redshift, it is strongly dependent on the limiting magnitude truncating the luminosity function. When $\rm M_{lim}$ is fixed, G(N) is approximately flat at statistically-representative samples of $\rm N\gtrsim 10$. Below $\rm N\sim 10$, G decreases slightly and errors on G become larger. We caution against making a flat richness cut (e.g., always calculating G using the 20 brightest members) on observed clusters, as this indirectly and imprecisely limits $\rm M_{lim}$.

Figure 3: The Gini index and mass gaps $\rm M_{*_{1,2}}$ and $\rm M_{*_{1,4}}$ applied to TNG300-1 Clusters 0 and 1 for 10 Gyr of assembly history traced by following the main progenitor branch of the BCG. We select and apply $\rm M_{*_{1,2}}$, $\rm M_{*_{1,4}}$, and G to the 20 brightest galaxies in each cluster at each timestep. The plotted markers are the mean and 1-sigma standard deviations of each indicator in 2 Gyr time bins spanning $\rm t_{age}\in[4~Gyr,14~Gyr]$, with horizontal error bars denoting the width of each bin. Each indicator shows the increasing trend expected from structural assembly and dynamical relaxation through time as BCGs grow more dominant, although $\rm M_{*_{1,2}}$ is nearly consistent with flat within its mean errors.

Figure 4: Fractional scatter about mean values of G, $\rm M_{{*}_{1,2}}$, and $\rm M_{{*}_{1,4}}$ calculated in Figure 3 for TNG300-1 Clusters 0 and 1. $\rm\sigma_{x}$ is the 1-sigma standard deviation on each indicator, x, within a 2 Gyr time period (denoted by the horizontal error bar on each marker). $\rm\sigma_{G}/\bar{G}<\sigma_{M_{*_{1,4}}}/\bar{M}_{*_{1,4}}<\sigma_{M_{*_{1,2}}}/\bar{M}_{*_{1,2}}$ for all times, which agrees with our understanding that sensitivity to the clusters dynamical state and degeneracies due to galaxy indexing drive more scatter in the magnitude gaps than the Gini index.

Figure 5: Samples and selection function. HST-SPT (with $\rm 1\sigma$ uncertainties on $\rm M_{500})$ and SDSS-Planck are plotted over the SPT-SZ 2500d, SPT-ECS, and Salvati et al. [111] Planck PSZ2 samples. Open HST-SPT markers represent clusters that were imaged by HST, but not used in the final sample (see further discussion in Section III.2). Our selection function is linear and has a slope of $\rm m=-2.5\times 10^{14}M_{\odot}/h_{70}$ consistent with expected cluster growth rates from simulations [45]. Progenitors of approximately Perseus to Coma mass clusters are selected between two intercepts at $\rm z=0$ : $\rm b_{lower}=5.35\times 10^{14}M_{\odot}/h_{70}$ and $\rm b_{upper}=7.5\times 10^{14}M_{\odot}/h_{70}$.

Figure 6: The left panel shows the HST-SPT stacked sample plotted in color-offset (observed - simulated red sequence colors) and absolute magnitude space. The right panel shows the FSPS simulated red sequences for the HST-SPT sample. The y-intercepts of the simulated red sequences scales strongly with redshift, while the slope remains relatively constant, fixed by our mass-metallicity relationship (Equation 4). An example color cut is shown, which uses a red sequence width $\rm width_{RS}=\pm 2\sigma_{RS}$ around the measured sample mean $\rm\mu_{RS}$. Despite our use of broad filters, our red-sequence modeling produces a well-defined red sequence and blue cloud for HST-SPT.

Figure 7:  The Gini index (upper) and Magnitude Gap (lower) vs. redshift of the HST-SPT and SDSS-Planck samples for three cluster center types and BCG color-cut permutations: BCG centers with All BCGs (non-RS+RS) (panel 1), light-weighted algorithm centers with all BCGs (non-RS+RS) (panel 2), and light-weighted algorithm centers with only RS BCGs (panel 3). We plot the best fit line (solid) with 16th and 84th percentile error regions (shaded) and fit intrinsic scatter (dashed) for each distribution. The redshift distribution of the Gini index is relatively similar across the cut permutations, with a weakly-decreasing trend consistent with non-evolution within $\rm 1\sigma$. $\rm M_{1,2}(z)$ features a fit fractional scatter that is $\rm\sim 7$ times greater than that of G(z), and is fit with a wider variety of linear profiles that are consistent with non-evolution within $\rm 1\sigma$. Our application of linear regression and the KS-test conclude that G and $\rm M_{1,2}$ are unevolving for $\rm z<1$, though the $\rm M_{1,2}$ result is noisier.

Figure 8: Cluster richness (N) vs. redshift for HST-SPT and SDSS-Planck. We plot the median richness in the redshift bins $\rm z\in[0.05,0.2],[0.2,0.6],[0.6,0.8],[0.8,1.0]$ in black, with standard errors on the median approximated by $\rm SE=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{N}}$. Horizontal error bars are used to represent the width of the redshift bin where the median is calculated. The decrease in N appears to be driven by proportionality with our decreasing $\rm M_{500}$ progenitor selection and the decreasing red galaxy fraction with cluster redshift (Butcher-Oemler effect), which is most pronounced for $\rm z\in[0.8,1.0]$. The difference in mean N in the lowest-z bins is driven by data availability and suggests the HST-SPT and SDSS-Planck samples are well-matched. While the declining RS-galaxy fraction causes N to approach values in the $\rm z\in[0.8,1.0]$ bin that drive G to decrease slightly (see Figure 2), this does not drive significant evolution of G in Figure
7.

Figure 9: Gini index vs. Fraction of Contamination ($\rm f_{cont}$), where G (Median – black line, shading – 68% and 95% C.I.s after 10,000 bootstrapping iterations) is calculated with its $\rm 1\sigma$ and $\rm 2\sigma$ errors for samples of $\rm N=100$ galaxies drawn from a “cluster” distribution of bright, red sequence core galaxies from HST-SPT and Planck-SDSS and a “field” distribution given by the Blanton et al. [15] luminosity function. Here, $\rm f_{cont}=0$ corresponds to the value of G calculated for a purely “cluster”-drawn sample, and $\rm f_{cont}=1$ corresponds to the value of G calculated for a purely “field”-drawn sample. The inset demonstrates the three-component Gaussian fitting of the color offset distribution used to estimate $\rm f_{cont}$ for the full HST-SPT sample, as well as HST-SPT split across three z-bins: $\rm z\in[0.2,0.6],[0.6,0.8],[0.8,1.0]$. While our measured $\rm f_{cont}$ is relatively high and increases with redshift, G is robust at the levels of contamination estimated in our cluster membership selection.

Figure 10:  The Gini index of cluster cores vs. the galaxy field. We reproduce panel 1 of Figure 7, where G is calculated for red sequence galaxies in BCG-centered cores of the HST-SPT and SDSS-Planck samples with all BCGs (non-RS+RS) included. We additionally calculate the median Gini index (blue lines) with 16th and 84th percentile C.I.s for several published luminosity functions (Blanton et al. [15] r-band, Bell et al. [9] r-band, and Faber et al. [44] for all galaxies), representing the full galaxy field.
We sample each luminosity function above the median cut applied to our observed data ($\rm M_{lim}=M^{*}+1.75$), and find that $\rm G_{field}$ and thus the shape of the full luminosity function does not evolve strongly over $\rm z\in[0,1]$. $\rm G>G_{field}$ and is non-evolving for the cluster cores across $\rm z\in[0,1]$, implying that BCGs are dominant and growing with the red sequence for $\rm z\leq 1$.

2611.18929.abstract: We introduce the Gini index (G) as a metric for studying the emergence of brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs) by quantifying the disparity in the light distribution of galaxy cluster cores. The Gini index collapses the skewness of the bright-end luminosity function to a single statistic, and provides a measure for the light dominance of the BCG over other cluster members that is more robust than the magnitude gap. We argue that the Gini index is far less sensitive to short-term changes in the cluster dynamical state than the magnitude gap and solves its known degeneracies by taking the entire cluster membership into account, making G a more sensitive metric to long-term BCG assembly. We apply the magnitude gap and Gini index to a progenitor-selected sample of 92 South Pole Telescope- and Planck-selected cluster cores at 0 < z < 1 with corresponding Hubble Space Telescope F110W and F200LP and Sloan Digital Sky Survey g and r photometry. Based on both parametric and empirical tests, we find no statistical evidence for evolution in G or $\rm M_{1,2}$ over 0 < z < 1, and find that BCGs have not grown significantly (2${\times}$) faster than the cluster population for z < 1 at 3${\sigma}$ confidence. This implies that BCGs achieve dominance and establish defining properties early (z > 1) in massive clusters. In general, we find that the Gini index is a valuable and relatively straightforward measurement, with well-controlled systematics, that could be applied to much larger samples to study BCG dominance and emergence.

2611.18980.title: Gradients of Turbulent Fluctuations as New Tracers of Astrophysical Magnetic Fields

figures.caption:
Figure 1: 
Schematic illustration of the local anisotropy of magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence, adapted from Pattle (2019). Alfvénic turbulent eddies become elongated along the local magnetic field, while turbulent mixing proceeds preferentially across the field. As a result, the strongest local velocity variation occurs perpendicular to the magnetic-field direction, producing velocity gradients that are preferentially perpendicular to the local field.

Figure 2: Scaling and anisotropy of the three MHD turbulent modes in low-$\beta$ turbulence, adapted from Cho and Lazarian (2003). The simulation has $\beta\simeq 0.2$, $M_{s}\simeq 2.3$, and $M_{A}\simeq 0.7$. Columns correspond to Alfvén, slow, and fast modes, respectively. The upper panels show the velocity and magnetic-energy spectra: Alfvén and slow modes follow approximately Kolmogorov-like $k^{-5/3}$ scalings, whereas fast modes are closer to a $k^{-3/2}$ spectrum. The middle panels show contours of the second-order velocity structure function measured relative to the local magnetic field. Alfvén and slow modes exhibit strong scale-dependent anisotropy, consistent with $r_{\parallel}\propto r_{\perp}^{2/3}$, while fast modes are approximately isotropic. The lower panels compare the structure functions measured parallel and perpendicular to the local magnetic field, further demonstrating the anisotropic Alfvén and slow cascades and the nearly isotropic fast-mode cascade.

Figure 3: Numerical illustration of velocity caustics. Panel (a) shows a synthetic PPV cube $\rho_{s}(x,y,v)$ generated from a spatially uniform density distribution and the LOS velocity field of a multiphase turbulence simulation. Panel (b) shows representative spectra at three positions in the projected map. Panel (c) shows the spatially averaged velocity spectrum and a representative velocity-channel map. The shaded region indicates the velocity interval used to construct the channel. Complex spatial structures appear despite the absence of internal density fluctuations, illustrating turbulent velocity mapping. Adapted from Hu et al. (Hu et al., 2023).

Figure 4: Illustration of the sub-block averaging procedure introduced by
Yuen and Lazarian (2017). The upper panels show the distributions of the
VCGs’ orientation (red) and the relative angle between the
VCGs and polarization (blue) in 16 sub-blocks of a synthetic
velocity centroid map. Although individual gradients exhibit substantial scatter, each sub-block develops a statistically preferred orientation; the peak of the gradient-angle distribution is used to determine the mean gradient direction. The lower panel compares the gradient directions recovered from sub-block averaging (red) with the synthetic polarization in the simulation (blue).

Figure 5: Comparison of the plane-of-sky magnetic-field morphology inferred from the
PCA-enhanced Velocity Gradient Technique (VGT-PCA) with that traced by Planck 353 GHz dust polarization in two large regions of the Galactic sky. The first and third panels show the magnetic-field orientations reconstructed with VGT-PCA, while the second and fourth panels show the corresponding Planck polarization-derived magnetic-field orientations. Streamlines indicate the inferred POS magnetic-field direction, and the dashed curves mark Galactic longitude and latitude. The close morphological agreement demonstrates that velocity gradients statistically recover the large-scale and local magnetic-field structure over extended diffuse H i regions. The corresponding alignment measures are ${\rm AM}=0.71\pm 0.02$ and $0.65\pm 0.01$ for the two regions, respectively. Adapted from Hu et al. Hu et al. (2020).

Examples of magnetic-field tracing with velocity gradients in molecular clouds under different dynamical conditions.

Magnetic-field orientations inferred from 12CO-VGT-VChGs (red segments in the left panel and yellow segments in the right panel) closely follow those derived from Planck 353 GHz ($\simeq 850\,\mu{\rm m}$) dust polarization (blue segments or streamlines). The 12CO-VGT-VChGs magnetic morphology (magenta) is compared with that inferred from Planck 353 GHz ($849\,\mu{\rm m}$) dust polarization (orange). The magnetic fields were inferred from Planck 353 GHz polarized dust emission (top) and the VGT-VChGs using ${}^{12}{\rm CO}$, ${}^{13}{\rm CO}$, and HNC emissions. We subtracted the foreground contribution from the Planck polarization and overlaid it on the total dust emission intensity map. The VGT-VChGs measurements are overlaid on corresponding integrated intensity colour maps. The contours on ${}^{12}{\rm CO}$ and ${}^{13}{\rm CO}$ intensity maps start from twice the mean intensity. Figure 8: Comparison of magnetic-field morphology in NGC 1097 inferred from CO-VChGs and independent polarization measurements. The left panel shows the large-scale field traced by 12CO$(2$–$1)$ VGT-VChGs together with SOFIA/HAWC+ 89 $\mu$m dust polarization; the color of the polarization segments indicates the local alignment measure between the two tracers. The upper middle and right panels zoom into the circumnuclear region and starburst ring, comparing the VGT-VChGs field (black streamlines) with HAWC+ 89 $\mu$m polarization (white segments). Adapted from Hu et al. (Hu et al., 2022).

2611.18980.abstract: Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence is ubiquitous in astrophysical plasmas and produces scale-dependent anisotropy with respect to the local magnetic field. Because turbulence cascades preferentially perpendicular to the field, its spatial gradients acquire preferred orientations that can be used to probe magnetic-field structure. This property underlies a family of gradient techniques based on spectroscopic, synchrotron-intensity, and synchrotron-polarization observations. In this review, we summarize the theoretical foundation of these techniques, including the anisotropy of MHD turbulence and the corresponding behavior of velocity, magnetic-field, and density fluctuations. We then describe how these fluctuations are encoded in spectroscopic data and synchrotron observables, and review the implementation of Velocity Centroid Gradients, Velocity Channel Gradients, Intensity Gradients, Synchrotron Intensity Gradients, and Synchrotron Polarization Gradients. We also discuss the effects of isotropic fast modes, shocks, self-gravity, stellar outflows, thermal broadening, and self-absorption. Finally, we review applications to the diffuse interstellar medium, star-forming regions, the Galactic center, external galaxies, and galaxy clusters.

2611.19211.abstract: Non-parametric statistics characterize complex galaxy morphologies but do not specify how to construct images that reproduce those statistics. We present Flow-VAE, which combines a variational autoencoder with a conditional normalizing flow to generate images conditioned on concentration, asymmetry, smoothness (CAS), Gini coefficient (G), and M20. A Gaussian mixture model completes unspecified descriptors and measures the training-distribution support of requested combinations. Using a dataset of 240,000 DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys r-band images, we evaluate fidelity by remeasuring morphological statistics from model outputs and comparing them with the inputs. With a tolerance of +/-10% of each descriptor's adopted range, descriptor-specific recovery rates are 96.62-99.97% for reconstruction and 87.81-99.83% for single-parameter generation among valid measurements. Generated descriptors show regression toward typical training values, while less-supported joint conditions produce broader residuals and systematic offsets. These results quantify the extent to which Flow-VAE can generate galaxy images consistent with prescribed non-parametric morphological statistics.

2611.19391.abstract: The Galactic disc is a complex dynamical system showing various kinematic structures, including moving groups (MGs), diagonal ridges (DRs), and velocity waves. To investigate their possible dynamical connection, we analyzed the phase-space distribution of stars from the extit{Gaia} DR3 catalog. We used angular momentum $L_z$ as a key dynamical tracer and examined stellar densities and velocities as functions of $L_z$. We identified stellar groups at specific $L_z$-values and associated them with extrema in the median radial velocity $\left<V_R ight>$, known as a velocity wave. By cross-matching the extrema of the $\left<V_R ight>$-wave with structures in the $V_R$--$L_z$ and $R$--$L_z$ planes, we established a clear connection between the velocity wave, the main MGs, and the DRs. A similar connection was partially identified for corrugations in the median vertical velocity $\left<V_z ight>$. Both velocity waves are strongest near the Galactic mid-plane and decrease in amplitude with increasing vertical distance. Our results demonstrate that MGs, DRs, and velocity waves in the solar neighborhood are different projections of the same dynamical structures associated with Lindblad and corotation resonances. These resonances arise from coupling between the radial and azimuthal stellar motions and are particularly prominent in the thin Galactic disc. Numerical simulations including perturbations from the Galactic bar and spiral arms confirm these conclusions. Our findings indicate that the local stellar disc is currently evolving in a state of dynamical equilibrium. We also show that in-plane velocity oscillations must be considered when interpreting vertical stellar distributions, as they may produce artifacts in vertical profiles.

2611.19491.abstract: Halo secondary bias describes the dependence of halo clustering on properties beyond mass. Here we report that a new environmental metric, the unbound matter fraction ($f_{\rm un}$) in the $2$--$3\,R_{\rm vir}$ shell around a halo, can largely account for secondary bias. Using haloes with $M_{\rm vir}=10^{10.5}$--$10^{14.5}h^{-1}{\rm M_\odot}$ at $z=0$ obtained from TNG300-1-Dark, we find that controlling for $f_{\rm un}$ reduces the secondary bias of formation time, concentration, spin, shape and velocity anisotropy to a residual correlation of $\lesssim 4\%$, outperforming other environmental metrics such as the tidal anisotropy for spin and velocity anisotropy. Applying a stacking method to the circum-halo medium (CHM), we identify two distinct flow patterns: low-$f_{\rm un}$ haloes co-move with coherent flows, with the CHM converging onto the haloes; in contrast, high-$f_{\rm un}$ haloes move through dynamically hot, partially virialized structures, with the CHM passing by rather than being accreted. This dichotomy points to two distinct regimes of secondary bias, a `cold' regime and a `hot' regime, in which tidal and inertial forces act as the main drivers, respectively, with the dominant mechanism migrating from the former to the latter as haloes assemble into massive structures. At fixed large-scale environment, $f_{\rm un}$ further indicates the presence of nearby neighbours and the competitive accretion. Our results highlight the role of unbound matter as a mediator of environmental effects on haloes, and reveal the physical mechanisms that shape the CHM pattern through which these effects are mediated.

2611.19631.abstract: Inspection of deep JWST images centered on the lensing cluster of galaxies MACS J0454.1-0300 reveals a small, well resolved stellar system that is clearly in the foreground. Photometric measurements including a color-magnitude diagram and radial profile show that it is a nucleated dwarf early-type galaxy (dE,N) at a distance of ~60 Mpc and with structurally normal properties. This object (J04:54:07.39-02:59:22.5, referred to as Orion I for shorthand) may be an outlying member of a previously known small galaxy group, or may be simply an isolated field galaxy depending on the accuracy of its distance estimate. The discovery of Orion I suggests that other small stellar systems in the nearby universe might be found through a search of the many deep \jwst imaging fields that are now being accumulated.

2611.19884.abstract: Galactic bars are important tracers of disk-galaxy evolution, yet reported bar fractions vary among observational studies and between observations and cosmological simulations. We compare bar statistics and properties in the IllustrisTNG simulations(TNG100 and TNG50 at z~0.1) with Sloan Digital Sky Survey(SDSS) galaxies at0.1<=z<=0.1264. We generate synthetic r-band TNG images,match SDSS observational conditions,and analyze mock TNG and real SDSS images using a common image-based framework of source segmentation,morphological classification, and isophotal ellipse fitting. For face-on late-type galaxies with log(M*/Msun)>10,the global bar fractions are 26.68+/-0.23%,24.96(-.76/+.78)%, and 13.42(-1.07/+1.15)% for SDSS,TNG100,and TNG50,respectively. TNG100 broadly agrees with SDSS over 10^10<~M*<~10^11.2Msun but shows a higher fbar at higher masses, whereas TNG50 remains lower than SDSS over most of10^10<~M*<~10^11.7Msun. Bulge-disk decompositions show fewer high-n bulges in TNG100 than in SDSS,particularly at high masses,but more in TNG50. These differences in bulge concentration may contribute to the different bar fractions. Bar length generally increases with stellar mass,and this trend depends little on the adopted bar-length definition. However, the outer ellipticity-decline estimator(R0.85max) yields systematically larger bar lengths than the ellipticity-peak estimator (R(eps,max)^bar). Massive TNG100 galaxies have more extended stellar disks than SDSS,which may contribute to their smaller relative bar lengths(Rbar/Re). 2611.20141.abstract: The mass distribution of early-type galaxies (ETGs) encodes key information about baryonic processes and dark-matter assembly. In this paper, we propose a new framework to investigate the mass-density profiles of ETGs and their evolution with redshift, based on the redshift distribution of strong gravitational lenses. We compile 200 galaxy-scale strong lensing systems with complete information, including lens and source redshifts, Einstein radii, and spectroscopic velocity dispersions. To account for the heterogeneous construction of the compiled sample, we model a lens-redshift-dependent selection function for each survey category. By combining the lens-redshift distribution with velocity dispersion function (VDF) and spherical Jeans-based mapping, we obtain population-level constraints on the total mass-density slope gamma in three lens-redshift intervals, marginalizing over the luminosity-density slope delta and the stellar orbital anisotropy beta. We find that the total mass density of ETGs remains close to isothermal at low and intermediate redshifts ($\gamma=2.00^{+0.07}_{-0.15}$ at 0 < z_l < 0.5 and $\gamma=1.96^{+0.16}_{-0.26}$ at 0.5 < z_l < 0.6), with a shallower effective slope at higher redshift ($\gamma=1.81^{+0.17}_{-0.21}$ at $0.6<z_l\lesssim1.0$). The marginalized posteriors of delta and beta remain broad, consistent with $\delta\simeq2$ and with isotropic orbits in all three redshift intervals. These results are consistent with the redshift trend predicted by Horizon-AGN simulations, in which active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback, together with stellar assembly and merging, contributes to the structural evolution of ETGs. Applied to the much larger lens samples expected from future missions such as the Chinese Space Station Telescope (CSST), this method will enable tighter tests of density-slope evolution and its connection to galaxy formation processes.

2611.20166.abstract: Strong gravitational-lensing systems with multiple source planes are powerful tools for probing the stellar and dark matter content of galaxies. Lens modelling can measure the relative Einstein radii of the two source planes, which encode a ratio of angular-diameter distances determined by the lens and source redshifts and the dark energy equation of state, independently of the Hubble constant. Galaxy-scale double-source-plane lenses (DSPLs) are extremely rare. We present a sample of 84 galaxy-scale DSPL candidates in Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1), of which 80 are newly identified. These systems were selected using machine-learning lens-finding models followed by visual inspection by citizen scientists and experts. We then used lens modelling to test the DSPL interpretation. Among our lens candidates, 11 form the 'Gold' sample: each shows two sets of multiple images at different radii, and the observed configuration is reproduced by a DSPL lens model. The remaining 73 'Silver' candidates have at least two lensed arcs from visual inspection, but either lack multiple images for at least one arc, have a best-fitting DSPL distance ratio close to the single-source-plane limit, remain compatible with a single-plane model with multiple sources, or have not yet been modelled. Even if all 84 candidates are DSPLs, the sample falls below the approximately 90 systems expected from extrapolating the Euclid Quick Data Release 1 (Q1) yield and the approximately 200 obtained by scaling the LensPop forecast to the DR1 area, indicating that many DSPLs remain undetected in DR1. Spectroscopy or higher-resolution imaging is required before we can be confident that the Silver candidates are DSPLs.

2611.20236.abstract: The biconical outflow of the nearby Seyfert 1.5 AGN NGC 4151 has been studied across the electromagnetic spectrum, yet mapping its multiphase structure with a single facility has remained challenging. Leveraging the broad wavelength coverage of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), we present new near- and mid-infrared observations tracing the ionization stratification of these outflows with a unified dataset. We analyze emission lines originating from molecular gas to highly ionized plasma and analyze the ionized gas using a 5-component Cloudy photoionization model covering three primary phases. Applying the footprint line method to characterize the X-ray emitting gas, we find that it holds the largest share of the total mass, suggesting that it is a primary candidate for driving AGN feedback in this system.

2611.20302.abstract: Normal shock waves are commonly described as mixtures of upstream and downstream Maxwellians. Discrete-velocity solutions of three relaxation models up to Mach 12 and direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) of hard-sphere and variable-hard-sphere gases up to Mach 25 are used to examine the population structure, Mach-number similarity and upstream precursor of their velocity distributions. Three anisotropic Gaussian populations reproduce the streamwise reduced distributions of the Bhatnagar--Gross--Krook (BGK) model and of DSMC to within 4\% up to Mach 12, and of DSMC to within 6\% at Mach 25, whereas two Maxwellians incur errors up to 50\% (BGK) and 37\% (DSMC). Collision histories identify the hard-sphere beam with unscattered stream molecules, which carry half of the peak viscous stress; the other populations are effective descriptions, not collision classes. Above Mach 5, Rankine--Hugoniot-scaled distributions are nearly Mach-independent, with corrections linear in $1/M^2$, consistent with the scaled kinetic equation. At equal normalised density, Mach 8 and 12 give the heat flux and stress at Mach 25 within 1\%, comparable to the accuracy of the reference; with one moment equation for position, physical-space profiles follow within 5\%. Comparing three prediction methods shows that the accuracy comes from the scaling; the Gaussian form adds compactness. Ahead of the shock, the mass of upstream-moving molecules decays as a stretched exponential with effective exponent 0.68--0.87. Collisions regenerate upstream-moving molecules, which explains a decay slower than free-flight survival; a linear cascade model with a downstream-Maxwellian source and no input from the shock interior reproduces the decay rates within 1.2\%.

2611.20358.abstract: We present a study of the compact-source population associated with the massive galaxy cluster MACS J1149.5+2223 at z=0.544 using deep JWST/NIRCam imaging in F115W, F150W, and F200W. After photometric and morphological selection, we identify 1,202 unresolved compact-source candidates. The observed luminosity distribution samples only the bright side of the expected globular-cluster luminosity function (GCLF), remaining several magnitudes above the turnover. Based on published GCLF turnovers for Abell 2744 and MACS 0417, we adopt an expected turnover magnitude of m_0=33.66 mag for MACS 1149. A forward-modeled fit then yields sigma=1.71 mag, which characterizes the observed bright-side slope under the adopted turnover rather than the intrinsic width of the full GCLF. Comparison with PARSEC simple stellar population models shows that the elevated luminosities of the compact sources are consistent with the expected fading of younger stellar populations as they evolve toward the present epoch. The brightest sources reach luminosities comparable to those of ultra-compact dwarfs. However, stellar-population degeneracies and possible foreground contamination make it difficult to distinguish. Together with recent JWST studies of globular cluster systems across a range of redshifts, MACS 1149 extends the emerging observational sequence of compact stellar systems and supports stellar population fading as an important contributor to their luminosity evolution across cosmic time.

2611.20633.abstract: Deriving stellar astrophysical parameters from large-scale spectroscopic surveys requires accurate modeling of spectra across a wide wavelength coverage and a broad range of stellar parameter space, which remains a great challenge. In this work, we present \texttt{TDSM}, a physically motivated neural network architecture that self-consistently emulates both the flux and its first-order derivative of the ab initio stellar spectra. The method enables accurate and precise emulation of Kurucz synthetic spectra with severely blended features at $R \simeq 2000$ in a high-dimensional parameter space, achieving a typical pixel-wise flux precision of 0.05\% in the wavelength range $3700<\lambda<9000$Å over the parameter range of $3000 < T_{\rm eff} < 45,000$~K, $-1 < \log g < 5$, and $-4.0 < \mathrm{[Fe/H]} < 0.5$. The model is applied to LAMOST DR10 to derive stellar parameters for 11 million spectra spanning the full model parameter range. We conduct detailed refinement and calibration efforts to mitigate systematic errors, which are revealed to be significant and complex due to imperfections in the ab initio model atmosphere. The resultant catalog provides eight stellar labels -- $T_{\rm eff}$, $\log g$, $v_{\rm mic}$, [Fe/H], [$\alpha$/Fe], [C/Fe], [N/Fe], and [Mg/Fe] -- for 8 million unique stars (11 million spectra including repeat observations) across the full parameter space. This adds a valuable dataset for studies of Galactic structure and archaeology, stellar populations, and related areas of astrophysics.

2611.20828.abstract: We present an overview of the LAMOST III Low-resolution Spectroscopic Survey (LRS), including its scientific goals, target selection strategy, and current observing status. Targets in the main survey are selected via weighted random sampling, using the inverse local density in the Hertzsprung-Russell (HR) diagram and in the G-magnitude distribution, with additional enhancement in selected regions of the HR diagram. The main survey is complemented by 35 dedicated add-on catalogs (including very metal-poor star candidates, halo stars, hot/young stars, wide binaries, extragalactic sources and so on) and a time-domain program providing multi-epoch spectroscopy of binaries and other peculiar systems. LAMOST III LRS is designed to map the structure and evolution of the Galactic disk, reconstruct the assembly and early chemical-enrichment history of the Galactic halo, improve stellar-parameter calibration, and characterize rare and variable objects. By June 2025, the LAMOST III LRS had obtained 1.53 million low-resolution spectra from 658 plates, corresponding to 1,264,052 unique sources. Relative to LAMOST I+II, the current sample is enriched in O/B stars, subgiants, main-sequence turn-off stars, metal-poor stars, and other previously underrepresented populations. In particular, the fractions of metal-poor and very metal-poor stars increase from 3.8% and 0.4% in LAMOST I+II to 9.0% and 1.1% in LAMOST III LRS, respectively, demonstrating the improved efficiency of the revised target-selection strategy for Galactic archaeology and stellar astrophysics.

2611.20884.abstract: Stellar orbits encode the dynamical history of galaxies and provide a physically motivated link between galaxy structures and assembly processes. Although orbit-based decompositions are well established in the Local Universe, their evolution across cosmic time, especially at higher redshifts, remains poorly explored. We investigate the orbital structure of \texttt{LEGA-C-like} galaxies in the \texttt{TNG100} simulation from $z=1$ to $z=0$ to identify how stellar mass, star formation activity, environment, merger history, gas content, and ex situ stellar mass growth shape their orbital transformation. We decomposed the stellar orbital structure of simulated galaxies into cold, warm, hot, and counter-rotating (CR) components using time-averaged orbital circularities. We find a strong mass dependence of orbital structure at $z=0$ as well as at $z=1$. Galaxies below $\log(M_\star/M_\odot)\sim11.2$ have a combined warm and cold orbital fraction of $\sim70\%$, whereas more massive systems have a hot-orbit fraction of $\sim60\%$. These trends are consistent with assembly pathways driven predominantly by wet and dry major mergers, respectively. Tracking the same galaxies to $z=0$ reveals a systematic, but mass-dependent, evolution toward lower rotational support: At both low and high stellar masses, the hot-orbit fraction increases, whereas the relative change is greater in low-mass galaxies. The survival of cold structure depends strongly on the star formation state at $z=1$; star-forming progenitors retain substantially larger cold fractions than the quiescent progenitors. At both redshifts, the orbital fractions show a rise (decline) in hot and CR (cold and warm) orbits with the ex situ stellar mass fraction at a fixed stellar mass. These results provide the first evolutionary framework for interpreting orbit-based decompositions of galaxies at the \texttt{LEGA-C} epoch.

2611.20917.abstract: The LAMOST Galaxy Parameter Catalog (LAGC) is a value-added data product of the LAMOST spectroscopic survey, generated by an automated spectral-fitting pipeline and released as a continuously updated catalogue series. Despite the vast data volume of the LAMOST spectroscopic survey, no dedicated, homogeneous pipeline had previously been able to extract stellar population, kinematic, and emission-line information simultaneously from its galaxy spectra, primarily because of the poorly controlled absolute flux calibration and a line spread function (LSF) that varies with wavelength, fibre, and time. The pipeline addresses both challenges through the SEW full-spectrum fitting method, which operates in equivalent-width space and is therefore immune to multiplicative flux-calibration errors, together with an accurate, wavelength-dependent model of the LAMOST LSF that enables unbiased kinematic measurements. As the pilot release of the catalogue series, we process the full galaxy sample of the latest LAMOST data release (283,691 spectra) and measure stellar population parameters, stellar and gas kinematics, and equivalent widths of 19 emission lines, each with bootstrap-based uncertainties. Repeat LAMOST observations confirm that the measurements are reproducible and that the bootstrap uncertainties are well calibrated, while comparison with SDSS shows only minor systematic offsets, attributable mainly to the SDSS LSF modelling. The measurements reproduce the well-established relations of the local galaxy population, and the catalogue will be publicly available and continuously updated as new observations become available. LAGC thus provides a reliable scientific catalogue for galaxy evolution studies, while the methodology behind it offers a blueprint for the next generation of fibre-fed spectroscopic surveys.

2611.20967.abstract: To investigate the processes governing clustered star formation, we present a multi-wavelength study of the star-forming complex hosting clusters Waterloo 01 and [BDS2003]64 in Sh 2-208. Both clusters exhibit elongated morphologies, with radii of $\sim1.5$ and $\sim0.9$ pc, respectively, and are located at a common distance of $\sim3.5$ kpc. Wat01 displays hierarchical structure ($Q=0.6$) and signature of mass segregation ($\Gamma_{\rm MSR}=1.5\pm0.6$). Its relaxation time, comparable to or longer than its age, suggests that the observed segregation may have a primordial contribution. The mass function follows a single power law, $\Gamma=-1.62\pm0.15$, over $\sim0.7$-$19.6$ M$_\odot$. Molecular-line observations reveal distinct velocity components associated with S208 and Wat01, indicating different molecular environments within the complex. Wat01 is strongly shaped by massive-star feedback, with an evacuated cavity, surrounding shell, and compressed globules consistent with an expanding H\,{\sc ii} region; feedback may have promoted localized star formation, although a direct causal connection cannot be established. In contrast, \textit{Herschel} data uncover a hub-filament system (HFS) in S208, with the central hub associated with BDS64 and the H\,{\sc ii} region powered by 'S1'. The filaments remain relatively well-preserved, indicating that gravity continues to play an important role in assembling dense gas toward the hub and in clustered star formation, even as feedback begins to affect the immediate surroundings. Overall, this complex illustrates the coexistence of feedback-processed and comparatively less-disrupted star-forming environments, highlighting the evolving interplay between stellar feedback and gravity in clustered star formation.

2611.20973.abstract: Using the centroid velocities of RGB stars and the individual velocities of O-B stars from the Gaia DR3, we test whether the spiral structure in the investigated region of the Galaxy can be described by a single wave with a constant pattern speed within the framework of Lin-Shu density-wave theory. The amplitudes of the radial and azimuthal velocity perturbations are determined for three centroid samples: centroids within strips 350 pc wide around five spiral arms; centroids within the same strips, with an additional condition on the radial gradient of the radial velocity, $M_{11}^+$; and all centroids within $5 \leq R \leq 15$ kpc and $130^\circ \leq \theta \leq 270^\circ$. The periodic and smooth non-periodic velocity components are fitted simultaneously. For each sample, the amplitudes derived from the RGB centroid velocities and the individual O-B stellar velocities are used to calculate the relative frequency as a function of Galactocentric radius, $R$, and subsequently the pattern speed at different radii. The analysis is performed for both stellar populations and for two assumed numbers of spiral arms, $m=4$ and $m=5$, using either the amplitude ratio or the radial amplitude alone. None of the cases considered supports a constant pattern speed within the adopted Lin-Shu model. We regard the pattern speed inferred from the radial solution for a specified perturbing potential as our main result. The estimate based on the amplitude ratio provides a complementary result that is consistent with the main conclusion of a non-constant pattern speed, but is less reliable because of the azimuthal response.

2611.21042.abstract: We investigate the fundamental kinematic parameters of stellar motions in the Milky Way using a statistical sample of 27,485,720 stars with measured three-dimensional velocities from the Gaia DR3 catalogue. From these data, we determine the local solar velocity $(U_{\odot},V_{\odot},W_{\odot}) = \left(10.5\pm0.7,14.5\pm0.9,7.33\pm0.1\right) ~\mathrm{km/s}$, the average rotation velocity\linebreak $\mathrm{V}_{0} = \left( 228\pm4\right) $ km/s, and the circular velocity $\mathrm{V}_{c} = \left( 234\pm4\right) $ {km/s,} both at the radius $R_{\odot}$. Next, within the range of $3-14$ kpc, we derive the Galactic circular velocity curve $\mathrm{V}_{c}(R)$ and determine the average spherical components of the stellar velocities as functions of both Galactocentric radius $R$ and distance from the Galactic plane $\left\vert Z\right\vert $. Two-dimensional $R-Z$ maps of these components reveal a complex three-dimensional kinematic structure. In particular, the pattern observed at $R\lesssim5$ kpc can be associated with the influence of the Galactic bar. To facilitate the description of the observations, we employ a simplified axisymmetric Monte Carlo model with several free parameters that reproduces the main kinematic trends.

2611.21175.abstract: Galactic Chemical Evolution (GCE) models connect stellar nucleosynthesis to observed abundance patterns, but their interpretation requires simultaneous parameter inference and comparison between competing stellar yield prescriptions. This remains challenging due to intractable likelihoods and growing dataset complexity. Using compass, a novel simulation-based inference framework, we perform, for the first time, amortized joint Bayesian model comparison and parameter inference for GCE models with intractable likelihoods within a unified architecture. Compass employs a conditional score-based diffusion model with a transformer architecture to learn both the posterior and likelihood directly from forward simulations, enabling efficient inference and likelihood-based ranking of competing nucleosynthetic yield sets. In controlled tests, compass identifies the generating yield set and recovers ground-truth parameters with accuracy comparable to existing simulation-based inference (SBI) methods, while reducing computational cost by orders of magnitude. Applied to Milky Way data, the framework favors a hybrid NuGrid + IllustrisTNG yield prescription, confirmed by an independent classifier, and infers an initial mass function slope of $\alpha_{\rm IMF} = -2.65 \pm 0.02$ and a SN$_{\rm Ia}$ normalization of $\log(N_{\rm Ia}) = -2.81 \pm 0.02$, with a systematic spread of $\approx 0.3$ in $\alpha_{\rm IMF}$ between the best-ranked yield sets, consistent with independent constraints. The attention mechanism confirms that the inferred parameters are driven by physically meaningful abundance signatures. By unifying amortized parameter inference, Bayesian model comparison, and interpretability in a single probabilistic framework, compass provides a scalable approach for precision chemical evolution studies with current and forthcoming spectroscopic surveys.

2611.21337.abstract: Primordial black holes (PBHs) may constitute a fraction of dark matter, but distinguishing them from black holes of stellar origin remains a major challenge. We propose a new method based on the three-dimensional localization of Galactic Binary Black Holes (BBHs) by the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA). While stellar-origin BBHs are expected to be associated with the stellar distribution of the Milky Way, PBHs may trace its more extended dark matter halo. We introduce a spatial overlap ratio that compares the gravitational-wave localization of each binary with the normalized stellar and dark matter density profiles. Using a Fisher-matrix forecast and 1000 Monte Carlo realizations of a 10-year LISA mission, we find that detecting three BBHs with an overlap ratio ln B < 0 occurs in approximately 99% of simulations where BBHs trace dark matter, but in fewer than 0.1% of simulations where they follow the stellar distribution, even when including a stellar halo containing 3% of the Galactic stellar mass. These results suggest that the localization of only a few Galactic BBHs could provide strong evidence for a primordial population, offering an independent test of their possible contribution to dark matter.

2611.21400.abstract: We present the discovery and characterisation of G195.65$-$0.10 (also known as the $\lambda$-complex), a giant hub-filament system identified by the Outer Galaxy High Resolution Survey (OGHReS). The complex contains 61 spatially and kinematically coherent HiGAL clumps with a mean velocity of $V_{\rm LSR}=32.85$ km/s and a velocity dispersion between clumps of 1.97 km/s. A $Gaia$ parallax measurement of the central emission-line star MWC 137 associated with an embedded cluster gives a heliocentric distance of 5.2$^{+0.8}_{-0.6}$ kpc, placing the complex at a Galactocentric radius of 13.2 kpc. The molecular structure spans approximately $35\times63$ pc and contains $\sim 1.6\times10^{5}$ M$_\odot$ of molecular gas, including $\sim 5 \times 10^{4}$ M$_\odot$ in dense clumps. The molecular emission is organised into three prominent velocity-coherent filaments that converge on a dense central hub. Of the associated clumps, 16 are protostellar and 45 are gravitationally bound but currently starless. The protostellar clumps are significantly more concentrated towards the hub than the starless population, with median projected offsets of 6.65 and 15.83 pc, respectively. Moreover, the luminosity-to-mass ratio of the protostellar clumps decreases significantly with increasing distance from the hub, indicating that the most evolutionarily advanced sources are preferentially located in the central region. These results reveal a systematic concentration of dense gas and increasingly evolved star formation towards the hub, with organised large-scale gas motions throughout the filamentary network. The $\lambda$-complex therefore provides an unprecedented laboratory to understand hierarchical and high-mass star formation in the outer Galactic disc.

2611.21580.abstract: The first generation of metal-free Population III (Pop~III) stars provides a possible formation channel for the black hole (BH) seeds in the early Universe. Their remnants may grow through gas accretion and mergers, producing gravitational wave (GW) signals detectable by future observatories. We develop a semi-analytical model of fragmentation in a primordial self-gravitating gas disk within minihaloes at $z > 15$, motivated by high-resolution cosmological simulations. The resulting Pop~III stars form around a central primary, some leaving massive BH remnants that migrate towards the central BH through dynamical friction from gas and dark matter, while the central BH grows through accretion and mergers. For a $10^6~{\rm M_\odot}$ halo at $z=20$, we explore how the initial mass function (IMF) and BH accretion efficiency affect detectability with the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) and the Einstein Telescope (ET). We find that both detectors can potentially reveal mergers of Pop III remnant BHs, but favor different astrophysical conditions. LISA pinpoints more massive central BHs ($\sim10^3$-$10^4 {\rm M_\odot}$), grown rapidly through mutual mergers alongside efficient gas accretion ($f_{\rm Edd}=1$), and a relatively top-heavy IMF ($\alpha=0.8$). In contrast, detectability with ET favors lower-mass BHs, with less efficient accretion ($f_{\rm Edd}=0.01$) and a steeper IMF ($\alpha=1.5$). These results highlight the potential of LISA and ET to probe Pop~III BH formation, growth, and mergers across different regions of parameter spaces, jointly constraining Pop~III star formation and early BH seed evolution.

2611.18943.abstract: The Affordable Multiple-Aperture Spectroscopy Explorer (AMASE) project aims to enable high-resolution spectroscopy of ionised gas in galaxies. However, fabricating ultra- dense fibre bundles with micrometre-level precision presents significant challenges. We detail a fabrication process that combines precision machining, stress-reducing handling, and iterative polishing. Although the final prototype did not meet the optical performance targets, our methods reduced manual labour, improved reproducibility, and identified critical failure modes, providing essential information for future astrophotonic instrument designs.

2611.19048.abstract: Multipeak fraction is a strong indicator of stellar multiplicity with subarcsecond angular separation in the Gaia DR3 catalog. We select 18 sources with multipeak fraction above 5% among stars possibly in the 20 pc solar neighborhood with as yet unconfirmed binarity. We successfully resolve eleven systems of M-type dwarf components in speckle interferometric observations with a 2.5 m telescope at the Caucasian Mountain Observatory of Sternberg Astronomical Institute, Moscow State University. 2611.19134.abstract: We analyze the microlensing event OGLE-2018-BLG-0829, whose light curve exhibits a weak short-term anomaly in addition to the prominent caustic-crossing features of a binary lens. The anomaly cannot be explained by a binary-lens single-source (2L1S) model. We therefore investigate both binary-lens binary-source (2L2S) and triple-lens single-source (3L1S) interpretations and find that both models reproduce the additional anomaly, with the 3L1S model being favored by $\Delta\chi^2=15.1$. Under the favored 3L1S interpretation, the anomaly arises from a caustic induced by a planetary-mass companion, whereas the prominent caustic-crossing features are produced by the underlying binary lens. Combining the measured event timescale, $t_{\rm E}=7.55\pm0.30$ days, and angular Einstein radius, $\theta_{\rm E}=0.325 \pm 0.059$ mas, with a Bayesian analysis, we infer a lens system consisting of an M dwarf of mass $0.193^{+0.300}_{-0.098}\,M_\odot$, a possible brown-dwarf companion of mass $0.068^{+0.105}_{-0.034}\,M_\odot$, and a Saturn-mass planet of mass $0.337^{+0.522}_{-0.171}\,M_{\rm J}$. The companions have projected separations of approximately 3.6 au and 1.6 au from the primary, respectively. However, the physical interpretation remains tentative because potentially important higher-order effects have not been considered, and the dynamical stability of the proposed configuration remains uncertain. If confirmed, this would be the third star--brown dwarf--planet system identified through microlensing, highlighting the potential of microlensing to detect planets in complex multiple systems.

2611.19327.abstract: We present a broadband X-ray spectral analysis of the radio galaxy Centaurus~A, utilizing simultaneous \textit{XRISM} (Resolve and Xtend) and \textit{NuSTAR} observations. Unlike the previous phenomenological analysis of the Fe K$\alpha$ line (Bogensberger et al. 2025), we employ physical reflection models developed with the radiative transfer code SKIRT. They self-consistently predict the continuum and fluorescent lines from a clumpy torus and an X-ray broad line region (xBLR). The Fe K$\alpha$ complex is well reproduced with a three velocity component model. We interpret this as two narrow torus components (FWHM $= 310\pm50$ and $1900\pm400$~km~s$^{-1}$) and an xBLR component (FWHM $= 6000_{-800}^{+1100}$~km~s$^{-1}$). The inner torus radius of 0.13~pc is 10 times the dust sublimation radius (0.013~pc), implying that the torus in a low-luminosity AGN is not determined by dust-related physics. The xBLR has a substantial covering factor of 0.11--0.36, a hydrogen column density ($5 \times 10^{23}$~cm$^{-2}$), a radius of 0.014~pc from the SMBH, and a mass of $>0.9 M_\odot$. Its mass supply rate is comparable to the accretion rate inferred from the bolometric luminosity, implying efficient xBLR formation even at low Eddington ratios. The xBLR line width also provides a novel estimate of the black-hole mass, $\log{(M_{\rm BH}/M_{\odot})} = 7.00\pm0.34$, via the optical BLR mass-scaling relation to the Fe~K$\alpha$. This agrees with dynamical measurements within a factor of $\sim5$, consistent with the scatter of the optical relation. We also infer the abundance ratios of $A_{\rm Ca}/A_{\rm Fe} = 1.1_{-0.1}^{+0.2}$ and $A_{\rm Ni}/A_{\rm Fe} = 1.4_{-0.2}^{+0.1}$ solar.

2611.19867.abstract: We investigate partial tidal disruptions of He and CO white dwarfs (WDs) by a $10^{4}\,M_{\odot}$ intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) using three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations. We construct realistic WD structures and abundance profiles with MESA and map them into FLASH to follow the remnant response and the time-dependent composition of the fallback debris in single pericentre passages on tightly bound orbits ($e=0.9$). The element-specific fallback rates exhibit pre-peak compositional transitions that trace the WD's stratified layers. In the grazing encounter ($\beta=0.55$), hydrogen dominates the earliest returning debris, followed by helium, showing a H$\rightarrow$He transition. Deeper encounters ($\beta=0.7$ and $0.8$) penetrate the CO core and produce a He$\rightarrow$C transition, that occurs earlier relative to peak fallback and is stronger in the deeper encounter. These signatures provide a potential spectroscopic diagnostic for identifying CO-WD tidal disruption events (TDEs). We then develop a semi-analytic model for repeated tidal stripping and predict passage-to-passage compositional evolution, in which the stripped material becomes progressively enriched in heavier elements as deeper layers are exposed, leading to stronger and earlier abundance transitions in later flares. We find that WDs can survive several dozen ($\sim 30$-$80$) passages, depending on their initial mass and compactness. Our results link time-dependent abundance signatures to repeating WD disruptions and provide testable observable predictions for identifying IMBH-powered transients.

2611.19906.abstract: Context. Magnetic fields are believed to play a crucial role in the launching, acceleration, and evolution of blazar jets. However, direct measurements of the magnetic field strength in the radio-emitting regions of blazar jets remain limited. Aims. We aim to estimate the magnetic field strengths in the synchrotron self-absorption (SSA) regions of blazar jets and investigate their connections with the properties of the jet and central engine. Methods. We compiled multifrequency radio data for 143 blazars and fitted their radio spectra with a combined power-law and SSA model to derive the turnover frequency and turnover flux density. The magnetic field strengths were then calculated by combining the SSA parameters with the very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) measured angular sizes and Doppler factors compiled from the literature. Results. The SSA-derived magnetic fields are systematically lower than those obtained from broadband spectral energy distribution modeling, suggesting that the two methods probe different regions of the jet. We further investigated the correlations between the SSA magnetic field strength and the apparent knot speed, {\gamma}-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and accretion disk luminosity. Only a weak correlation is found between the SSA magnetic field strength and {\gamma}-ray luminosity, while the best-fit relations with the other investigated parameters also exhibit negative slopes, suggesting a common tendency that is qualitatively consistent with magnetic energy being progressively converted into bulk kinetic energy during jet propagation. Conclusions. Our work presents a large statistical studies of SSA-derived magnetic fields in blazars and provides new observational constraints on the magnetic evolution of relativistic jets.

2611.20416.abstract: Gravitational waves (GWs) from a stellar-mass binary black hole (BBH) orbiting a supermassive black hole (SMBH) can experience repeated gravitational lensing as the BBH passes behind the SMBH. Our previous studies of orbit-induced GW modulation motivate this investigation of repeated lensing in evolving hierarchical triple systems. We investigate how eccentricity, inclination, and relativistic precession of the outer orbit affect successive lensing events and parameter inference. The outer orbit follows post-Newtonian dynamics, and the inspiral waveform includes moving-source effects and de Sitter precession. An event-local point-mass lensing model tracks the changing source--lens alignment and GW frequency. For a one-year LISA observation, we examine lensing-event identification, Fisher-matrix estimates of parameter uncertainties, and waveform residuals when lensing is omitted. Our results show that outer-orbit evolution changes the timing and amplification of successive lensing events and can bring initially unfavorable configurations into the lensing region. A fixed circular, nonprecessing approximation misses all lensing events for a substantial fraction of the selected lensed systems. The median fractional reductions in uncertainty are largest for the outer-orbit inclination and SMBH spin. For some systems above the adopted detection threshold, lensing-induced waveform differences persist after local adjustments to the parameters of the unlensed model. Repeated lensing can thus provide complementary constraints on SMBH properties and outer-orbit geometry in LISA observations of hierarchical BBHs.

2611.20418.abstract: A new epoch for direct visualisation of accretion dynamics near a black hole's event horizon began when the Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration (EHTC) synthesised an Earth-sized aperture with millimeter radio interferometry and published the first reconstructed image of a black hole shadow at the core of radio galaxy Messier 87 (M87). The image appeared as a ring-like structure, representing the gravitationally lensed and redshifted emission around the central supermassive black hole, M87*, located at the galactic nucleus. However, application of various data analysis and imaging heuristics resulted in divergent representations of M87* fine-scale features, with some external analyses even challenging the fundamental ring-like morphology of the source. Such difficulties arise as a consequence of the inherent sparsity of the very-long baseline interferometry (VLBI) measurements, rendering interferometric image reconstruction an inadequately constrained problem. Moreover, the solution is sensitive to instrument calibration, post-processing algorithms, and imaging hyperparameters. Here, we apply a newly-developed independent imaging algorithm to the M87* dataset, which is free from prescriptive morphological priors and founded on observables immune to instrument calibration errors. We reconstruct the black hole shadow image, and unequivocally reproduce a ring-like morphology, with angular diameter 42.2 +/- 1.5 microarcseconds corresponding to a black hole mass of 6.5 +/- 0.5 billion solar masses assuming nominal scaling parameters, observed at an inclination angle of ~20 deg from the approaching jet.

2611.20636.abstract: The $Gaia$ high-resolution spectroscopic observations using Radial Velocity Spectrometer offers a unique opportunity to study stellar Ca II infrared triplet (IRT) activity. A key step in estimating activity indices is subtracting the photospheric contribution. The canonical template-based method often fails because, for many stars, the observed line cores are deeper than the model predictions, which prevents valid activity measurements. In this work, we explore an alternative approach that constructs a baseline from less active stars as a function of effective temperature (and metallicity) to represent the photospheric contribution. Our results show that, for dwarf stars, compared with the canonical method, the baseline method not only yields far more objects with valid activity measurements, but also avoids many extremely low and unreliable values (e.g., log$R'_{\rm IRT} \lesssim -6$). The Ca II IRT activity indices derived from the baseline method correlate well with other activity proxies, confirming their reliability as activity indicators. Furthermore, they show a relation with stellar rotation, not only recovering the typical rotation--activity relation, but also revealing fine structures that may be associated with different regimes in gyrochronology. Our findings suggest that the baseline method can serve as a robust alternative for deriving accurate activity estimates, and will be particularly useful for obtaining activity indices for tens of millions of stars with the upcoming $Gaia$ Data Release 4.

2611.20669.abstract: The nature of progenitor systems of Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) and their explosion mechanism remain controversial. Radio observations provide a powerful probe of the interaction between SN ejecta and circumstellar material (CSM), offering important constraints on the mass-loss histories of their progenitor systems. We present extensive Jansky Very Large Array (JVLA) observations of SN 2020eyj at 1.5-10 GHz, tracing its radio emission to approximately 1300 days after discovery and revealing, for the first time, the long-term radio evolution of an SN Ia. The radio light curves of SN 2020eyj exhibit a relatively flat evolution at early epochs, followed by a gradual long-term decline, while its radio spectra show a power-law behavior with a low-frequency turnover. These characteristics appear to be consistent with synchrotron emission associated with shock interaction. Modeling the radio light curves favors a thick circumstellar shell with an inferred mass of approximately 0.3-0.4 solar masses over the simple wind-like configurations. Combined with the optical spectral signatures of SN 2020eyj, our radio observations provide strong evidence for substantial helium-rich mass loss from the progenitor system prior to explosion. The inferred CSM properties pose significant challenges to existing SN Ia progenitor models, although the ejection of a common envelope shortly before explosion may offer a plausible explanation.

2611.20672.abstract: Radio observations of supernovae (SNe) enable us to constrain the circumstellar environment of their progenitor stars, and hence the mass-loss history immediately prior to the explosion. However, despite lines of evidence pointing to the aspherical configurations of circumstellar matter (CSM) around many SNe, the derivation of CSM parameters is often done under the assumption of spherically symmetric CSM. In this work, based on a recent model of radio emission from SNe interacting with aspherical CSM, we investigate how lifting the assumption of spherical symmetry affects the CSM parameter inference. First, we apply the model to mock data simulating typical observations of Type Ia-CSM, Ibc and II SNe and find that the total CSM mass required for to reproduce radio observation depends weakly on the CSM covering fraction $f_\Omega$, with ${f_\Omega}^{0.15-0.38}$. We then apply the model and fit the radio light curves of Type Ia-CSM SN 2020eyj. We show that, even with the assumption of asphericity as severe as $f_\Omega = 0.1$, the requirement for the total CSM mass is only reduced to $\sim 50 \%$ of the value inferred in spherical models. These results demonstrate that introducing asphericity in radio emission models is often not enough to reduce the required CSM mass significantly.

2611.21128.abstract: Classical Cepheids (CCs) are standard candles and key tracers of young stellar populations. However, their use in the most obscured regions is hampered by the high interstellar extinction at optical wavelengths. Near-infrared spectroscopy offers major advantages by greatly reducing absorption corrections and enabling access to regions of the Milky Way that are still poorly sampled. In this work, we determine the atmospheric parameters and abundances of Fe, Mg and Si for a sample of 27 CCs based on observations with ERIS@VLT in J-band low-resolution mode ($R \sim 4000$). Combining PySME with 1D MARCS atmosphere models and non local thermal equilibrium grids, we simultaneous optimise the atmospheric parameters through spectral fitting. This method is validated with a direct comparison with high-resolution optical investigations and re-analysis of archive optical spectra for the targets in common. The results show good consistency in both metallicity and chemical abundances. We obtain mean abundance ratios of $\mathrm{\langle[Mg/Fe]\rangle=0.01\pm0.12~dex}$ and $\mathrm{\langle[Si/Fe]\rangle=0.10\pm0.09~dex}$, in agreement with reference samples. Moreover, we provide for the first time the Mg and Si abundances of 12 CCs. Finally, we have found distinct kinematic properties for two of the most distant Galactic CCs, located at Galactocentric distances of $\mathrm{\approx 28-29~kpc}$ and with extreme values of vertical height, $\mathrm{\approx +4.8~kpc}$ and $\mathrm{\approx -5.3~kpc}$; more data are required to constrain their nature. Our results confirm that J-band spectroscopy at low-resolution can be used as a good diagnostic for the chemical investigation in highly obscured Galactic regions, otherwise inaccessible at optical wavelengths.

2611.21350.abstract: The astrophysical site of the rapid neutron-capture process ($r$-process) is still one of the major open questions in astronomy. A key mystery is the origin of the peculiar actinide-to-lanthanide ratio found in the so called actinide-boost stars, with $ \rm \log \epsilon (Th/Eu)>-0.35$. Here we present the largest sample of Th measurements in stars formed in an external galaxy, Gaia Sausage Enceladus. From this sample, we present the three most metal-rich actinide-boost stars discovered to date, $\rm -1.6<[Fe/H]<-1.1$. In addition, we measured Th in a comparison sample of Milky Way stars formed in situ, and compiled Th measurements from the literature which do not account for non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) effects. After applying NLTE corrections to the combined sample, a bimodality in the $\rm\log\epsilon (Th/Eu)$ ratio is revealed. Unexpectedly, actinide-boost stars lie on a very narrow $(\sigma=0.02)$ plateau of $\rm \log\epsilon(Th/Eu)=-0.2$, clearly separated from actinide-normal stars. Most (if not all) of the actinide-boost stars in our sample originate from outside the Milky Way. Chemical evolution models show that such a plateau can arise, even at [Fe/H] = $-$1, when a single actinide-rich event dominates the r-process content of a small or gas-depleted system. Combined with other evidence, our results suggest that mergers with neutron stars are the most promising astrophysical site for actinide-boost stars.

2611.21353.abstract: The reduced speed of light approximation (RSLA) is a common approach in radiation-hydrodynamic (RHD) simulations of non-relativistic systems where the gas speed $v_{\rm gas} \ll c$. In the RSLA one eases the severe time step constraint imposed by the speed of light $c$ by replacing it with a reduced value $\hat{c}$ chosen so that $v_{\rm gas} \ll \hat{c} \ll c$. This approach works well in flows with low or moderate optical depth, but fails in optically thick media, where it makes thermal relaxation too slow and gives incorrect RHD wave modes. Here we propose an Adaptive Reduced Speed of Light Approximation (ARSA) that removes these problems by replacing the global speed reduction factor $\phi_0 \equiv \hat{c}/c$ with a local, cell-by-cell reduction factor $\phi$ derived from a von Neumann stability analysis of the implicit-explicit update used by modern two-moment RHD codes. The resulting limiter has no tunable parameters, can be computed using only local operations, and improves on the classic RSLA by allowing $\phi \to 1$ in cells where a reduced speed of light is not required because the exchange with the gas damps unstable modes, allowing recovery of the correct thermal relaxation and wave-damping rates in highly-opaque regions. We compare ARSA to the classic RSLA in a range of standard RHD test problems, and show that in opaque regions where gas holds most of the heat capacity the ARSA is much more accurate than the RSLA at the same time step, or that it can achieve the same accuracy as the RSLA with up to 100 times fewer time steps. However, gains are limited in regions where radiation holds a large share of the heat capacity, as it does in some astrophysical systems.

2611.21510.abstract: Gaia has observed every detected source on the sky 50 to 100 times, each time through a window of about 1 by 2 arcseconds at a different scan angle. The resulting one-dimensional flux profiles to be released in Gaia DR4 encode the two-dimensional arrangement of nearby point sources at ~0.1 arcsecond resolution. Repeated observations also constrain their relative motion. We present a method to model the scene with a mixture of moving point sources. Complementing Gaia DPAC's source-environment reconstruction, our approach focuses on close, blended companions and models their relative motion. We first fit each window with a few point sources and obtain their along-scan positions. We then triangulate these positions from different scan angles to identify candidate sources on the sky. A joint forward model of all windows measures positions, fluxes, relative proper motions, and parallax differences, even for blended components. In simulations, we recover companions at separations smaller than the instrumental profile width. For a moving companion at ~75 mas separation with a flux ratio of ~0.2, we obtain a separation precision of ~0.1 mas and a relative proper-motion precision of ~0.1 mas/yr per component, even in a scene contaminated by a third source. These precisions assume a known instrumental profile and independent Gaussian noise. We also recover differential parallax for a chance-aligned source. Modeling nearby contaminants prevents significant biases. With a Gaia-like instrumental profile, sampling and scan law, we show a sensitivity of ~5 mag in contrast at separations of 50-150 mas, and we discuss its dependence on the color term of Gaia's line-spread function. The method could extend the census of close companions and provide relative astrometry, and so dynamical information, along short orbital arcs. External measurements could also guide retrospective searches in Gaia's windows.

2611.21534.abstract: Context. Li-rich stars are rare, and only 16 are known in globular clusters (GCs), spanning evolutionary stages from the main sequence turnoff to the red giant branch. Their origin is still debated, but GCs provide a unique environment to discriminate among proposed mechanisms for Li enrichment. Aims. We aim to characterise two newly discovered Li-rich dwarf stars, 44606 and 58195, in the GC M 4 (NGC 6121) and investigate their origin among the formation channels proposed in the literature. The previously known Li-rich star in the cluster, namely 37934, was re-analyzed for comparison. Methods. We performed a standard abundance analysis based on 1D model atmospheres in local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) on high-resolution Ultraviolet and Visual Echelle Spectrograph (UVES). We measured the projected rotational velocity and searched for chromospheric activity. Results. We derive A(Li)= 2.58, 2.51 dex for stars 44606 and 58195, respectively, significantly different from the A(Li) distribution of normal dwarfs in M 4. For the known Li-rich star 37934, we obtain A(Li)= 3.01 dex, consistent with previous work. We estimate detailed abundances of 24 species (Li, C, N, O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, S, K, Ca, Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Sr, Y, Zr, Ba, and Nd) in the three stars. None of our targets show detectable rotational broadening or chromospheric activity. Conclusions. The Li-rich stars analysed here are unevolved, ruling out in-situ Li production. Planet engulfment is very unlikely in GCs, and we detect no present-day rotation or activity. By exclusion, the most plausible remaining scenarios involve different types of interaction with a companion, including dynamical interactions, mass transfer, and mergers. Currently, we have not detected a companion.

2611.21583.abstract: Galactic chemical evolution (GCE) predicts large-scale variations in exoplanet compositions with host star elemental abundances, reflecting the Milky Way's history of star formation and elemental enrichment from stellar feedback. We investigate the impact of GCE on the compositions of exoplanetary bodies using polluted white dwarfs (WDs), which probe the bulk elemental abundances of planetary debris. Using a literature sample of 70 polluted WDs, we calculate iron mass fractions for the accreted bodies and compare these to tracers of the WD progenitor's initial abundances, including age and kinematics. We demonstrate predicted trends using a sample of main sequence stars, and we show that these are generally reflected in the polluted WD sample. In particular, H-dominated WDs show preferentially larger iron mass fractions amongst younger and less dynamically excited systems. This trend is weaker amongst He-dominated WDs, and we show that this may be attributed to uncertainties in their observed phases of accretion. Continuing to combine WD pollution compositions with stellar parameters and kinematics could be a valuable way to constrain large-scale versus local drivers of planetary compositions.
